beats.narration: Begin by framing Foundations of Computation as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. This course provides an introduction to the theory of computation, including formal languages, grammars, auto-mata theory, computability, and complexity. Consider this worked case: A finite automaton accepts the string 'abab' by transitioning through states that track alternating 'a' and 'b' characters. On screen, display a state diagram with labeled transitions for a DFA that accepts alternating 'a' and 'b' strings, highlighting the start and accept states. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Foundations of Computation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a state diagram with labeled transitions for a DFA that accepts alternating 'a' and 'b' strings, highlighting the start and accept states.

beats.narration: Now define Formal Languages and Grammars precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Consider this worked case: A context-free grammar defines valid arithmetic expressions by recursively combining terms and operators. On screen, show a parse tree for the expression '3 + 4 * 2' with labeled non-terminals and terminal nodes. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Formal Languages and Grammars
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a parse tree for the expression '3 + 4 * 2' with labeled non-terminals and terminal nodes.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Automata Theory Basics operates in a concrete sequence. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. Consider this worked case: A pushdown automaton recognizes nested parentheses by pushing symbols onto a stack and popping them during matching. On screen, illustrate a pushdown automaton with a stack diagram showing push/pop operations during parenthesis matching. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Automata Theory Basics
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a pushdown automaton with a stack diagram showing push/pop operations during parenthesis matching.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Computability Limits and make the decision criteria explicit. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Consider this worked case: The halting problem demonstrates that no general algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary program will eventually stop. On screen, present a flowchart showing the decision tree for the halting problem, ending in an undecidable branch. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Computability Limits
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a flowchart showing the decision tree for the halting problem, ending in an undecidable branch.

beats.narration: Apply Complexity and Resource Bounds to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Consider this worked case: A sorting algorithm with O(n log n) time complexity processes larger inputs more efficiently than O(n^2) alternatives. On screen, plot two curves on a log-log graph comparing O(n log n) and O(n^2) growth, labeling the axes and intersection point. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Complexity and Resource Bounds
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Plot two curves on a log-log graph comparing O(n log n) and O(n^2) growth, labeling the axes and intersection point.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Loop Invariants and Proofs, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Consider this worked case: In a binary search, the invariant states that the target value, if present, lies within the current search interval. On screen, show a table tracking the search interval bounds and the invariant statement across three iterations of binary search. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Loop Invariants and Proofs
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a table tracking the search interval bounds and the invariant statement across three iterations of binary search.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Divide-and-Conquer Strategy with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Consider this worked case: Merge sort splits an array into halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves into a complete sorted array. On screen, display a recursive tree diagram showing array splits and merge steps for a 4-element array. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a recursive tree diagram showing array splits and merge steps for a 4-element array.

beats.narration: Use Recurrence Relations to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Consider this worked case: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) describes the time complexity of merge sort, solving to O(n log n). On screen, show a recurrence tree with labeled nodes for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn, summing the work at each level. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Recurrence Relations
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a recurrence tree with labeled nodes for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn, summing the work at each level.

beats.narration: Connect Graph Algorithms and Reachability to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Consider this worked case: Breadth-first search finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph by exploring neighbors level by level. On screen, render a directed graph with BFS traversal order highlighted, showing visited nodes and edge directions. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Graph Algorithms and Reachability
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a directed graph with BFS traversal order highlighted, showing visited nodes and edge directions.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space. Consider this worked case: Before implementing a sorting routine, verify the preconditions, prove the loop invariant, and derive the recurrence for time bounds. On screen, list a three-step checklist: 1) Define inputs/outputs, 2) Prove correctness via invariants, 3) Analyze complexity with recurrences. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | List a three-step checklist: 1) Define inputs/outputs, 2) Prove correctness via invariants, 3) Analyze complexity with recurrences.

A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. sources.excerpt: OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.
